title: Argumentative, Discursive and Reflective Essays
summary: The differences between argumentative, discursive and reflective essays, structuring an argument with evidence, linking words, counter-arguments, and writing a reflective essay.

rows: Persuade the reader to agree with ONE side
One-sided; your opinion is clear throughout
Discuss BOTH sides fairly before reaching a balanced conclusion
Balanced; opinion only (if at all) in the conclusion
Think about a personal experience, feeling or idea and what you learned from it
'A lesson I learned the hard way'

items: **Introduction**: introduce the topic and state your **thesis** (main position) clearly.
**Body paragraphs** (usually three): each paragraph makes **one point**, starting with a **topic sentence**, supported by **evidence** (facts, statistics, examples, expert opinion) and explanation.
**Counter-argument and rebuttal**: acknowledge an opposing view and show why it is weaker.
**Conclusion**: restate your position in new words and end with a strong final thought or call to action.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: A useful pattern for body paragraphs is **PEEL**: **P**oint, **E**vidence, **E**xplanation, **L**ink (back to your thesis).

rows: however, on the other hand, nevertheless, although
for example, for instance, such as
therefore, as a result, consequently, because
in conclusion, to sum up, ultimately

notes.title: Example argumentative paragraph (original)
notes.text: Firstly, a longer school day would leave learners exhausted rather than educated. Research on adolescent sleep shows that teenagers already struggle to get the eight to ten hours they need. Adding another hour of lessons would mean less time for homework, chores and rest, so learners would arrive at school even more tired. Therefore, extending the school day is likely to harm, not help, learners' results.

items: Written in the **first person**, often in the past tense for events and present tense for reflections.
Describes an experience, then **reflects** on it: How did I feel? Why? What did I learn? How have I changed?
Honest, thoughtful tone; may use figurative language.
The focus is on **insight**, not just on telling a story.

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Grade 9 essays are usually **300 to 350 words**. Include a plan, give the essay a title, and make sure each paragraph has a clear focus.

questions.prompt: Match each essay type to its purpose.

pairs.right: Persuade the reader to accept one side
Present both sides in a balanced way
Explore a personal experience and what you learned

questions.prompt: What is the statement of your main position in an argumentative essay called?

questions.memo:
✓ It shows you understand the opposing view (1)
✓ and by rebutting it you make your own argument stronger and more convincing (1)

questions.prompt: In a discursive essay, your personal opinion should dominate every paragraph.

✓ It is factual and supports the point, making it more convincing than opinion alone (1)

questions.prompt: Write an introduction for an argumentative essay on 'Learners should be allowed to use cellphones in class.'
questions.memo:
✓ Introduces the topic (1)
✓ Clear thesis stating one side (1)
✓ Engaging opening / outline of arguments; formal register (1)

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a narrative essay and a reflective essay?
questions.memo:
✓ A narrative essay mainly tells a story (1)
✓ A reflective essay focuses on thinking about an experience and the insight or lesson gained (1)
